content.user_title: Build Reliable Go Caches with samber/hot
content.value_statement: Repeated backend reads can increase latency and overload services. This skill guides samber/hot cache design with workload-based eviction, expiration, loaders, concurrency controls, and monitoring.
actual_capabilities: Compare nine eviction algorithms and recommend options based on recency, frequency, scan resistance, and memory constraints.
Guide typed cache construction with TTL, janitor lifecycle management, loader callbacks, and loader error handling.
Estimate entry capacity from memory budgets, key sizes, value sizes, and bookkeeping overhead.
Explain stale revalidation, negative caching, loader chains, and startup warm-up patterns.
Guide sharding and copy-on-read or copy-on-write configuration for concurrent workloads.
Show Prometheus collector registration and queries for hit ratio, eviction rate, and capacity usage.
limitations: Requires a Go project and the samber/hot dependency; the skill describes support for Go 1.22 or later.
Provides guidance and examples, not a running cache service or persistent distributed storage.
Cannot guarantee latency, hit rate, or memory usage without application measurements and representative benchmarks.
Examples require application-specific types, loaders, imports, and checks against the installed library version.

use_cases.title: Reduce Repeated Profile Queries
use_cases.description: Design a typed user cache with expiration, batch loaders, error handling, and negative caching for missing profiles.

use_cases.title: Investigate Cache Contention
use_cases.description: Review measured mutex contention, evaluate sharding, and choose monitoring signals before changing capacity or eviction policy.

use_cases.title: Review Cache Integration Safety
use_cases.description: Check janitor cleanup, incompatible builder options, stale-data policies, and shared mutable values during code review.

prompt_templates.title: Create a Basic Cache
prompt_templates.prompt: Using samber/hot, create a string-to-byte-slice cache with 10,000 entries and a five-minute TTL. Include janitor cleanup and handle retrieval errors.
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner: add a bounded cache with explicit expiration.

prompt_templates.title: Choose an Eviction Policy
prompt_templates.prompt: Compare samber/hot eviction policies for [access pattern]. Use [memory budget] and [estimated entry size] to estimate capacity. Explain what measurements would validate the choice.
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate: select an algorithm and estimate memory requirements.

prompt_templates.title: Protect a Database Loader
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a samber/hot cache for [entity] with a batch database loader and negative caching. Address concurrent misses, expiration jitter, loader errors, and janitor cleanup.
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced: reduce repeated backend work while preserving explicit error behavior.

prompt_templates.title: Review a Production Cache
prompt_templates.prompt: Review [cache implementation] against [freshness requirements], [concurrency profile], and [memory budget]. Evaluate sharding, revalidation, mutable values, Prometheus metrics, and shutdown. Propose focused validation tests.
prompt_templates.scenario: Expert: evaluate interacting cache configuration and lifecycle choices.

output_examples.input: Which policy fits stable, heavily skewed DNS cache lookups?
output: LFU is a candidate because a small, consistently popular key set dominates requests.
Changing popularity can leave outdated items favored, so compare alternatives if the workload shifts.
Benchmark representative lookups and choose TTL independently from eviction policy.

output_examples.input: Can I combine disabled locking with background TTL cleanup?
output: The skill identifies disabled locking and janitor cleanup as incompatible options that can panic.
Keep locking when using background cleanup or concurrent access.
For a single-goroutine design, omit the janitor and plan explicit cleanup.

output_examples.input: How should I monitor a samber/hot cache?
output: Enable the library's Prometheus metrics and register the cache as a collector.
Track hit ratio, eviction rate, and cache occupancy relative to capacity.
Set alert thresholds from workload requirements and investigate changes before increasing memory.

best_practices: Measure access patterns and entry sizes before selecting an eviction policy or capacity.
Set expiration deliberately, handle loader errors, and stop janitor goroutines during shutdown.
Validate concurrency and mutable-value handling with tests, then monitor hit ratio and eviction behavior.
anti_patterns: Disable locking for concurrent workloads or combine disabled locking with a background janitor.
Call negative-cache methods before enabling missing-key cache configuration.
Ignore loader errors or let callers mutate shared cached objects without suitable copying.

faq.question: What does this skill provide?
faq.answer: It provides samber/hot usage guidance, algorithm comparisons, API references, production patterns, and evaluation scenarios for Go cache work.

faq.question: Which AI tools are listed as supported?
faq.answer: The marketplace metadata lists Codex and Claude Code. The skill also describes compatibility with similar coding agent environments.

faq.question: Does this replace Redis or provide persistence?
faq.answer: No. The guidance targets process-local in-memory caching, although loader examples can retrieve data from Redis or a database.

faq.question: Which eviction algorithm should I start with?
faq.answer: The skill recommends W-TinyLFU for mixed or unknown access patterns. Use measured workload characteristics to evaluate specialized alternatives.

faq.question: How does it address simultaneous cache misses?
faq.answer: It explains loader-based singleflight deduplication and expiration jitter. You must still implement appropriate backend access and error handling.

faq.question: Does it automatically install dependencies or configure monitoring?
faq.answer: The files provide installation and monitoring examples. Applying them requires agent actions or developer changes within the project.
